newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish PM wins vote, bruised but unbeaten.
newsitem.headline: Swedish PM wins vote, bruised but unbeaten.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson on Friday survived a parliamentary vote of no-confidence over his China policy which he admitted had shaken but not weakened his ruling Social Democrats.
Three opposition parties had filed the motion against Persson after he failed to withdraw remarks which they said gave comfort to China's policy of suppressing internal dissent.

Despite his comfortable 204-119 vote victory, with 16 abstentions and 10 deputies absent from the 349-seat Riksdag, Persson admitted that the episode might have damaged the minority government's standing in the short term.
"We're going to get caned in the opinion polls," a rueful Persson told reporters in parliament after the morning vote.
But he added: "The government emerges from this stronger. Now that we're back to really big issues like unemployment there is a good majority in parliament."

The Conservative, Liberal and Christian Democratic parties pressed for the no-confidence vote, arguing that Persson's comments during an official visit to China this month had damaged Swedish interests.
He had told Swedish businessmen in Beijing: "To me, it's striking what political stability means for economic development when you look at the Chinese example."
Political commentators said Friday's vote had more to do with Swedish political manoeuvring than an ideological debate about the rights and wrongs of how to address China.

They noted that Conservative Party leader Carl Bildt, absent on an international mission in Bosnia, had nevertheless entered the fray by saying Persson's remarks should be seen as a one-off gaffe, effectively undermining his own party's stance.

"The only winner in this is Carl Bildt," the conservative Svenska Dagbladet wrote this week, comparing favourably his own professional diplomacy while prime minister with what it called Persson's bungling.

Defending himself in a special parliamentary debate on Wednesday, Social Democratic leader Persson said the whole affair had been exaggerated, and added: "I never placed any value judgement on the phrase 'political stability'."

Social Democrat Sven Hulterstrom, speaking before Friday's vote, warned parliament that a successful vote against Persson would cause a government crisis and accused the opposition of trying to score points.
Per-Ola Eriksson of the Centre Party said bringing a no-confidence vote against the prime minister was disproportionate to the criticism his China remarks had aroused.
The Centre and Leftist deputies lined up with the Social Democrats in Friday's vote.

Since the last election in 1994, the Social Democrats have ruled as a minority government with the tacit support of the Leftist Party, but Persson did not rule out a more formal coalition with the Centre.
"I am not averse to the idea," Persson told TV4 on Friday when asked about the possibility of a coalition with Centre.
"Even though there are ideological differences, the Centre and Social Democrats are very close and, as society evolves, we are getting even closer," he said.
Foreign Minister Lena-Hjelm Wallen denied suggestions that the vote had diminished Sweden's standing abroad.
"Not in the least. The whole world can see this is no more than a domestic game, a game with the constitution for short-term political capital," she said.
Christian Democrat leader Alf Svensson said he did not regret sponsoring the ill-fated no-confidence motion.
"Persson will think before he opens his mouth in future," Svensson said on TV4.
